title: Implement a stack using an array — push (add to top), pop (remove from top), peek (look at top without removing).
shortTitle: Implement a stack using an array

s1_definition.profdef: Implementing a stack with an array uses a backing array plus a `top` index that points at the current top element, starting at minus one for an empty stack. Push increments `top` and writes the element; pop reads the element at `top` and decrements; peek reads at `top` without changing it. All three are O(1). When the array fills, you resize by copying into a larger array, giving amortised O(1) push.
s1_definition.analogy: National Bank of India tracks Rajesh's recent in-session actions in a numbered tray with a marker that shows the top slot. Pushing an action puts it in the next slot and moves the marker up. Popping takes the action from the marker's slot and moves the marker down. Peeking just reads the marker's slot. When the tray is full, the clerk moves everything to a bigger tray and keeps going.
s1_definition.oneliner: Use an array plus a top index starting at minus one; push writes and moves top up, pop reads and moves top down, peek reads without moving.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Implementing a stack with an array uses a backing array plus a `top` index that points at the current top element, starting at minus one for an empty stack. Push increments `top` and writes the element; pop reads the element at `top` and decrements; peek reads at `top` without changing it. All three are O(1). When the array fills, you resize by copying into a larger array, giving amortised O(1) push.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** National Bank of India tracks Rajesh's recent in-session actions in a numbered tray with a marker that shows the top slot. Pushing an action puts it in the next slot and moves the marker up. Popping takes the action from the marker's slot and moves the marker down. Peeking just reads the marker's slot. When the tray is full, the clerk moves everything to a bigger tray and keeps going.

**One line to remember:** Use an array plus a top index starting at minus one; push writes and moves top up, pop reads and moves top down, peek reads without moving.

sections.s2_technical:
The two pieces of state are the backing array and the `top` index. An empty stack has `top` equal to minus one, meaning no element is on the stack. The number of elements is always `top + 1`.

Push first checks whether the array is full, which happens when `top + 1` equals the array length. If full, it resizes by allocating a new array of double the size and copying the elements over, then it increments `top` and stores the new element at `array[top]`. Doubling on resize is what gives amortised O(1): although an individual resize costs O(n), it happens rarely enough that the average push cost stays constant.

Pop first checks `isEmpty`, which is `top == -1`; popping an empty stack must throw because there is nothing to remove. Otherwise it reads `array[top]`, optionally nulls that slot to help garbage collection, decrements `top`, and returns the value. Peek also checks `isEmpty` and then returns `array[top]` without changing `top`. All three operations touch a single index, so each is O(1) apart from the occasional resize. A senior nuance is that a fixed-capacity stack that refuses to resize would instead throw a stack-overflow style exception when full, which is the right choice when you want a hard bound on memory.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — National Bank of India tracks Rajesh's recent in-session transaction amounts in a stack so the most recent can be reviewed or reversed first. The system must support push, pop, and peek on an array-backed stack. This is exactly how an array stack works with a top index.

Problem 2 — The session can accumulate more actions than the initial array holds, so the stack must grow without losing data. This is exactly why push resizes by doubling the array when full, giving amortised constant-time pushes.

The code has an `ArrayStack` class holding a BigDecimal array and a top index, with push, pop, peek, isEmpty, and size, plus automatic resizing. The demo exercises all operations including a resize.

sections.s5_journey:
Input: a stack with initial capacity 2, then push 1000, 2000, 3000, then pop twice.

Step 1 — Start empty, top is minus one, capacity 2.

Step 2 — push 1000: not full, top becomes 0, data[0] is 1000.

Step 3 — push 2000: not full, top becomes 1, data[1] is 2000. The array is now full because top plus one equals length.

Step 4 — push 3000: full, so resize doubles capacity from 2 to 4 and copies 1000 and 2000. Then top becomes 2 and data[2] is 3000. Size is now 3.

Step 5 — peek returns data[2] which is 3000, without changing top.

Step 6 — pop reads data[2] (3000), clears the slot, decrements top to 1, returns 3000.

Step 7 — pop reads data[1] (2000), clears the slot, decrements top to 0, returns 2000.

Step 8 — peek now returns data[0] which is 1000. isEmpty is false because top is 0, so size is 1.

```
2026-10-26 18:58:41 [INFO] Size after 3 pushes: 3
2026-10-26 18:58:41 [INFO] Peek top: Rs.3000.00
2026-10-26 18:58:41 [INFO] Pop: Rs.3000.00
2026-10-26 18:58:41 [INFO] Pop: Rs.2000.00
2026-10-26 18:58:41 [INFO] Peek top now: Rs.1000.00
2026-10-26 18:58:41 [INFO] Is empty? false
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```text
  capacity=2, top=-1 (empty)
    │ push 1000 → data=[1000,_]        top=0
    │ push 2000 → data=[1000,2000]     top=1 (FULL)
    │ push 3000 → resize 2→4, copy
    │             data=[1000,2000,3000,_]  top=2
    ▼
  peek → data[2]=3000 (top unchanged)
  pop  → 3000, data[2]=null, top=1
  pop  → 2000, data[1]=null, top=0
  peek → data[0]=1000
  isEmpty? top=0 → false
```
sections.s5d_lld:
```
  ═══ LLD — Array-Backed Stack ═══

  ┌─ Key Concept ────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  State: backing array + top index (-1 = empty).          │
  │  push: resize-on-full (double) → amortised O(1).         │
  │  pop/peek: O(1); null the slot on pop to help GC.        │
  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ── Class Diagram ───────────────────────────────

  ┌───────────────────────────────────────┐
  │              ArrayStack               │
  │───────────────────────────────────────│
  │ - data: BigDecimal[]                  │
  │ - top: int   (-1 when empty)          │
  │───────────────────────────────────────│
  │ + push(amt): void   O(1) amortised    │
  │ + pop(): BigDecimal O(1)              │
  │ + peek(): BigDecimal O(1)             │
  │ + isEmpty(): boolean                  │
  │ + size(): int  (= top + 1)            │
  └───────────────────────────────────────┘

  ── State: top index during run ──────────────────
  empty top=-1 → push×3 (resize) top=2 → pop×2 top=0

  Contract for push(amt):
    Pre:  none
    Post: amt is new top; array doubled if it was full
    Complexity: amortised O(1)

  Contract for pop():
    Pre:  not empty (top >= 0)
    Post: removes + returns top; slot nulled
    Throws: IllegalStateException if empty
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Implementing a stack with an array uses two pieces of state: a backing array and a top index that points at the current top element and starts at minus one when the stack is empty. The number of elements is always the top index plus one. Push increments the top index and writes the element there, pop reads the element at the top index and then decrements it, and peek reads at the top index without changing it. Each of these touches a single index, so they are constant time.

The one subtlety on push is capacity. When the array is full, I resize by allocating a new array of double the size and copying the elements over, then I store the new element. Doubling is important because although an individual resize costs linear time to copy, it happens rarely enough that the average cost of a push stays constant, which we call amortised constant time.

In my banking project at National Bank of India, I used an array-backed stack to track Rajesh's recent in-session transaction amounts, so the most recent can be reviewed or reversed first, and the stack grows automatically as the session accumulates more actions. I always check whether the stack is empty before popping or peeking, because operating on an empty stack must throw rather than return garbage. I also null out the slot when I pop, so the array does not hold a stale reference that would stop the garbage collector from reclaiming the object. If I needed a hard memory bound instead of automatic growth, I would make the stack fixed-capacity and throw an overflow exception when full rather than resizing, and I would choose based on whether a bounded or unbounded stack fits the requirement.
